arXiv:2603.06138v1 [cs.LG] 06 Mar 2026

Partial Policy Gradients for RL in LLMs

Puneet Mathur Affiliation: Adobe Research Correspondence to: puneetm@adobe.com    Branislav Kveton Affiliation: Adobe Research    Subhojyoti Mukherjee Affiliation: Adobe Research    Viet Dac Lai Affiliation: Adobe Research
Abstract

Reinforcement learning is a framework for learning to act sequentially in an unknown environment. We propose a natural approach for modeling policy structure in policy gradients. The key idea is to optimize for a subset of future rewards: smaller subsets represent simpler policies, which can be learned more reliably because their empirical gradient estimates are more accurate. Our approach allows for modeling and comparison of different policy classes, including full planning, greedy, KK-step lookahead, and segment policies. We evaluate the policies empirically on multiple persona-alignment conversational problems. Different policies excel in different problems, reflecting their different characteristics and highlighting the importance of our studied policy class.

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning (RL) (Sutton and Barto, 1998) is a framework for learning to act sequentially in an unknown environment with the goal of maximizing future rewards. Due to its generality and broad applicability, RL has been studied extensively and many RL algorithms have been proposed, including temporal-difference learning (Sutton, 1988), Q-learning (Watkins and Dayan, 1992), policy gradients (Williams, 1992), and actor-critic methods (Sutton et al., 2000). RL is more data demanding than supervised learning because it plans for the future (Sutton and Barto, 1998). Therefore, many early works on planning and RL tried to increase the statistical efficiency of learning algorithms by assuming additional structure, such as a known model of the environment (Bellman, 1957; Boutilier et al., 1995; Koller and Parr, 1999), linear value or Q functions (Tsitsiklis and Van Roy, 1997; de Farias and Van Roy, 2003; Hauskrecht and Kveton, 2004), and baseline subtraction in policy gradients (Sutton et al., 2000; Baxter and Bartlett, 2001; Munos, 2006).

Proximal policy optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017) and group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) are arguably the most popular RL algorithms for large language models (LLMs) (Ouyang et al., 2022). PPO is a policy gradient algorithm where the advantage is estimated using a per-token reward model. When the policy is learned from off-policy data, the advantage is corrected by clipped propensity scores (Horvitz and Thompson, 1952; Ionides, 2008). The challenge with applying PPO in practice is that a per-token reward model has to be learned. GRPO is a policy gradient algorithm where the advantage is estimated by simulation, which eliminates the need for a per-token reward model. The challenge with applying GRPO is that the advantage is attributed equally to all tokens, potentially reducing statistical efficiency.

We propose a natural approach for introducing policy structure in policy gradients. The first step is decomposing the total reward additively over time. This decomposition may be a part of problem definition, for instance when the problem is a Markov decision process (MDP) with per-step rewards (Bellman, 1957; Puterman, 1994), or obtained by a simple algebraic transformation. The second step is optimization for subsets of future rewards. The subsets lead to simpler policies than full planning, which can be learned more reliably because their empirical gradient estimates are more accurate. We propose both online and offline algorithms for learning our policies, and analyze them. Full planning, greedy, and KK-step lookahead policies are all instances of our framework.

LLMs are increasingly used to simulate human personas for social role-play (Tseng et al., 2024; Jandaghi et al., 2024). Despite that, off-the-shelf LLMs frequently drift from their assigned personas, contradict to their earlier statements, or abandon role-appropriate behavior (Ji et al., 2025; Abdulhai et al., 2025). We apply our policies to LLMs to maintain consistent and faithful human personas in role-playing dialogues. This problem is challenging because many dialogues have long horizons, on average 2020 steps and up to 6060. Our results show that KK-step lookahead policies lead to consistent personas in extended dialogues, mitigating the persona drift that plagues base models.

We make the following contributions:

  1. 1.

    We propose a framework for modeling policy structure in policy gradients. The key idea is to optimize for a subset of future rewards, which can be either observed or obtained by a simple algebraic transformation. Our formulation is more general than those in the closest related works, which focused only on specific policies (Kveton et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025), sometimes even without observations.

  2. 2.

    Our framework trades off the complexity of learned policies for the statistical efficiency of learning them. Specifically, optimization for smaller subsets of future rewards leads to learning simpler policies, which can be learned more reliably because their empirical gradient estimates are more accurate. We propose both online and offline algorithms for learning the policies.

  3. 3.

    We instantiate the framework: online policy gradient (Williams, 1992), policy gradient for adaptive submodular policies (Kveton et al., 2025) and segment-level credit assignment Guo et al. (2025), can be all viewed as instances of our framework. This is the first work that proposes and empirically evaluates KK-step lookahead policies in LLMs.

  4. 4.

    We empirically evaluate our policies on four persona-alignment conversational problems across multiple domains: education, therapy, chatting, and generic. We experiment with three LLMs: Qwen (Yang et al., 2025), Llama (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and Gemma (Team et al., 2025). We show that KK-step lookahead policies lead to consistent persona across extended dialogues (Section 5.4) by preventing persona drift (Section 5.5). The optimal value of KK depends on the domain camplexity and the amount of training data (Section 5.6).

The paper is organized as follows. We present our setting in Section 2. In Section 3, we present our framework for optimizing a subset of future rewards, interpret it, and analyze it. We instantiate the framework in Section 4 and evaluate it empirically in Section 5. Related works are reviewed in Section 6, and we conclude in Section 7.

2 Setting

We start with introducing our notation. The marginal and conditional probabilities under the probability measure pp are p⁡(X=x)p(X=x) and p⁡(X=x∣Y=y)p(X=x\mid Y=y), respectively; and we write p⁡(x)p(x) and p⁡(x∣y)p(x\mid y) when the random variables are clear from context. The indicator function is {⋅}\mathds{1}\!\left\{\cdot\right\}. For a positive integer nn, we define [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\left\{1,\dots,n\right\}. We denote the ii-th entry of vector vv by viv_{i}. If the vector is already indexed, such as vjv_{j}, we write vj,iv_{j,i}.

We consider a general reinforcement learning problem (Sutton and Barto, 1998) where an agent interacts with an environment in an episode consisting of multiple steps. The agent takes actions conditioned on the interaction history and the environment responds. When the episode ends, it is assigned a reward. The reward measures the quality of the interaction and the agent maximizes it.

We formalize the problem as follows. The agent first observes context x∈𝒮x\in\mathcal{S}, where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the space of all token sequences. The context defines the task. The interaction between the agent and environment consists of steps indexed by t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}, where ℕ\mathbb{N} is a set of positive integers. At step tt, the agent takes an action at∈𝒮a_{t}\in\mathcal{S} and the environment responds with an observation yt∈𝒮y_{t}\in\mathcal{S}. The interaction history up to step nn is a trajectory τn=(a1,y1,…,an,yn)\tau_{n}=(a_{1},y_{1},\dots,a_{n},y_{n}) of nn actions and observations. We assume that the number of steps nn is fixed. The reward is a non-negative function of xx and τn\tau_{n}, denoted by r⁡(x,τn)≥0r(x,\tau_{n})\geq 0, and measures the quality of the interaction. We do not make any additional assumptions on the reward. This is to maintain generality and because our algorithms (Section 3) do not require it.

The agent follows a policy conditioned on its history. Specifically, the probability that action aa is taken in context xx and history τt−1\tau_{t-1} is π⁡(a∣x,τt−1;θ)\pi(a\mid x,\tau_{t-1};\theta), and is parameterized by θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta. We call θ\theta a policy and Θ\Theta the space of policy parameters. The probability of observing yty_{t} conditioned on history τt−1\tau_{t-1} and action ata_{t} is denoted by p⁡(yt∣x,τt−1,at)p(y_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1},a_{t}). We slightly abuse our notation and denote the probability of trajectory τn\tau_{n} in context xx under policy θ\theta by

π⁡(τn∣x;θ)=∏t=1np⁡(yt∣x,τt−1,at)​π​(at∣x,τt−1;θ).\displaystyle\pi(\tau_{n}\mid x;\theta)=\prod_{t=1}^{n}p(y_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1},a_{t})\,\pi(a_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1};\theta)\,.

The factorization follows from the chain rule of probability. The expected value of policy θ\theta, where qq is a distribution over contexts xx, is defined as

V(θ)=𝔼x∼q,τn∼π(⋅∣x;θ)[r(x,τn)].\displaystyle V(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim q,\,\tau_{n}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x;\theta)}\left[r(x,\tau_{n})\right]\,. (1)

Our goal is to learn a policy θ∗=arg​maxθ∈Θ⁡V​(θ)\theta_{*}=\argmax_{\theta\in\Theta}V(\theta) with the highest expected value. Our formulation is more general than those in the closest related works, which focused only on specific policies and did not consider observations (Kveton et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025).

Our framework can model multiple use cases. For instance, suppose that we want to maximize the pedagogical value of a conversation over nn steps (Scarlatos et al., 2025). Then τn\tau_{n} is an nn-step conversation and r⁡(x,τn)r(x,\tau_{n}) is its pedagogical value. We experiment with such problems in Section 5. In math reasoning problems (Shao et al., 2024), τn\tau_{n} would be agent’s reasoning and r⁡(x,τn)r(x,\tau_{n}) would indicate whether its response is correct.

3 Algorithms

This section has four main parts. In Section 3.1, we introduce policy gradients. In Section 3.2, we present partial policy gradients. We interpret them in Section 3.3 and introduce offline partial policy gradients in Section 3.4.

3.1 Policy Gradient

We want to maximize the expected policy value V⁡(θ)V(\theta) in (1). While this can be done many ways (Sutton and Barto, 1998), the most straightforward method for complex policies, like those represented by LLMs, are policy gradients (Williams, 1992). The key idea in an online policy gradient is to update the policy θ\theta iteratively by gradient ascent. The gradient of V⁡(θ)V(\theta) at θ\theta is

∇V​(θ)\displaystyle\nabla V(\theta) =𝔼[r(x,τn)∇logπ(τn∣x;θ)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[r(x,\tau_{n})\nabla\log\pi(\tau_{n}\mid x;\theta)\right] (2)
=𝔼⁡[r⁡(x,τn)​∑t=1n∇log⁡π​(at∣x,τt−1;θ)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[r(x,\tau_{n})\sum_{t=1}^{n}\nabla\log\pi(a_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1};\theta)\right]\,,

where 𝔼[⋅]=𝔼x∼q,τn∼π(⋅∣x;θ)[⋅]\mathbb{E}\left[\cdot\right]=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim q,\,\tau_{n}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x;\theta)}\left[\cdot\right] is an expectation over the same random variables as in (1). This identity can be derived by a direct application of the score identity (Aleksandrov et al., 1968).

All policy gradient algorithms in this work are variants of the meta algorithm in Algorithm 1. The gradient in Line 10 is estimated from a batch ℬ\mathcal{B} of trajectories (Line 9) of size BB, which are sampled in Line 7 and assigned rewards in Line 8. We denote the ii-th trajectory in ℬ\mathcal{B} by τi,n\tau_{i,n}; and its context and reward by xix_{i} and rir_{i}, respectively. The gradient estimator for the classic online policy gradient is

g⁡(ℬ)=1B​∑i=1Bri​∑t=1n∇log⁡π​(ai,t∣xi,τi,t−1;θ).\displaystyle g(\mathcal{B})=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}r_{i}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\nabla\log\pi(a_{i,t}\mid x_{i},\tau_{i,t-1};\theta)\,. (3)

We refer to this instance of Algorithm 1 as 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG.

3.2 Partial Policy Gradient

While the gradient in (2) is valid, the reward is attributed equally to each step, since all ∇log⁡π​(at∣x,τt−1;θ)\nabla\log\pi(a_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1};\theta) are multiplied by the same reward r⁡(x,τn)r(x,\tau_{n}). If the attribution could be improved, we could reduce the variance in estimator (3) and improve statistical efficiency. We propose a general attribution framework that allows for such tradeoffs. The framework has two components.

Factored reward. We assume that the reward factors as

r⁡(x,τn)=∑t=1nrt,r1,…,rn≥0,\displaystyle r(x,\tau_{n})=\sum_{t=1}^{n}r_{t}\,,\quad r_{1},\dots,r_{n}\geq 0\,, (4)

where rt=r⁡(x,τt)r_{t}=r(x,\tau_{t}) denotes the reward at step tt, and is a function of xx and τt\tau_{t}. The reward rtr_{t} with such properties can be either observed, for instance if the environment is an MDP with per-step rewards, or designed. We present a general design that guarantees (4) next.

Lemma 1.

Let f⁡(x,τt)f(x,\tau_{t}) be any function of xx and τt\tau_{t} such that 0=f⁡(x,τ0)≤⋯≤f⁡(x,τn)=r⁡(x,τn)0=f(x,\tau_{0})\leq\dots\leq f(x,\tau_{n})=r(x,\tau_{n}). Let

rt=f⁡(x,τt)−f⁡(x,τt−1)\displaystyle r_{t}=f(x,\tau_{t})-f(x,\tau_{t-1})

hold for all t∈[n]t\in[n]. Then ∑t=1nrt=r⁡(x,τn)\sum_{t=1}^{n}r_{t}=r(x,\tau_{n}) and rt≥0r_{t}\geq 0 for all t∈[n]t\in[n].

The proof of the claim is in Section A.1. Since f⁡(x,τt)f(x,\tau_{t}) can be viewed as a trajectory reward up to step tt, rtr_{t} is the per-step gain in the total trajectory reward at step tt. If ff is not monotone, a monotone f¯\bar{f} can be obtained by a transformation f¯​(x,τt)=maxℓ∈[t]⁡f⁡(x,τℓ)\bar{f}(x,\tau_{t})=\max_{\ell\in[t]}f(x,\tau_{\ell}). Because of this, and without loss of generality, we assume that rt≥0r_{t}\geq 0 in the rest of our paper, unless stated otherwise. One natural choice of ff is an LLM judge (Zheng et al., 2023) that can judge partial trajectories. Similar decompositions were proposed before in more specific problems, without observations (Guo et al., 2025) and in optimization of submodular policies (Kveton et al., 2025).

Reward attribution. We consider a general partial policy gradient of the form

𝔼[∑t=1n(∑ℓ∈ℛtrℓ)∇logπ(at∣x,τt−1;θ)],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{R}_{t}}r_{\ell}\right)\nabla\log\pi(a_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1};\theta)\right]\,, (5)

where ℛt⊆[n]∖[t−1]\mathcal{R}_{t}\subseteq[n]\setminus[t-1] are reward indices affected by action at step tt through ∇log⁡π​(at∣x,τt−1;θ)\nabla\log\pi(a_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1};\theta). Specifically, ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} is the subset of future steps whose rewards are affected by ata_{t} conditioned on the history. The gradient can be estimated empirically as g⁡(ℬ)=g(\mathcal{B})=

1B∑i=1B∑t=1n(∑ℓ∈ℛtri,ℓ)∇logπ(ai,t∣xi,τi,t−1;θ),\displaystyle\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{R}_{t}}r_{i,\ell}\right)\nabla\log\pi(a_{i,t}\mid x_{i},\tau_{i,t-1};\theta)\,, (6)

where τi,n\tau_{i,n} is the ii-th trajectory in batch ℬ\mathcal{B}; and ai,ℓa_{i,\ell}, ri,ℓr_{i,\ell}, and τi,ℓ−1\tau_{i,\ell-1} are the action, reward, and trajectory history at step tt of this trajectory, respectively. When (6) is used in Algorithm 1, we call it partial policy gradient (𝙿𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPG) since only a subset of future rewards is used in policy optimization. Note that 𝙿𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPG reduces to 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG when ℛt=[n]∖[t−1]\mathcal{R}_{t}=[n]\setminus[t-1] for all t∈[n]t\in[n], as we show in Section 4.1. Our framework allows us to reason about other ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} and understand associated statistical tradeoffs.

𝙿𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPG is more statistically efficient than 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG, and we prove this formally in Section A.2. Specifically, Theorem 5 says that a partial policy gradient estimator g⁡(ℬ)g(\mathcal{B}) that optimizes for a subset of rewards of another estimator g′​(ℬ)g^{\prime}(\mathcal{B}) concentrates at 𝔼⁡[g⁡(ℬ)]\mathbb{E}\left[g(\mathcal{B})\right] faster that g′​(ℬ)g^{\prime}(\mathcal{B}) concentrates at 𝔼​[g′​(ℬ)]\mathbb{E}\left[g^{\prime}(\mathcal{B})\right]. The key idea in the proof is to treat (6) as a sum of random vectors, independent across ii but dependent across tt. Then we use Hoeffding’s inequality, which is a standard tool in concentration analyses (Raginsky and Sason, 2012; Boucheron et al., 2013), to argue that the sum of a subset of random vectors concentrates faster than the sum of the original set, when the vectors are sampled from the same distribution.

3.3 Interpretation

We interpret gradient ascent with respect to (5) next. That requires additional notation. Let 𝒮t={ℓ∈[t]:t∈ℛℓ}⊆[t]\mathcal{S}_{t}=\left\{\ell\in[t]:t\in\mathcal{R}_{\ell}\right\}\subseteq[t] be action indices that affect the reward at step tt, rtr_{t}. Note that by definition,

∑t=1n(∑ℓ∈ℛtrℓ)∇logπ(at∣x,τt−1;θ)\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{R}_{t}}r_{\ell}\right)\nabla\log\pi(a_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1};\theta) (7)
=∑t=1nrt​∑ℓ∈𝒮t∇log⁡π​(aℓ∣x,τℓ−1;θ).\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{n}r_{t}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\nabla\log\pi(a_{\ell}\mid x,\tau_{\ell-1};\theta)\,.

This is because we can first sum over log-probabilities and then over the associated rewards, or the other way around. Figure 1 illustrates ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} and 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} in full, greedy, and KK-step lookahead policies in Section 4. We also define St¯=[t]∖𝒮t\bar{S_{t}}=[t]\setminus\mathcal{S}_{t}, the complement of 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} with respect to the first tt steps. For any 𝒮,𝒵⊆[n]\mathcal{S},\mathcal{Z}\subseteq[n], we define

𝔼𝒮​[⋅]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}}\left[\cdot\right] =𝔼x∼q,τ𝒮∼π(⋅∣x;θ)[⋅],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim q,\,\tau_{\mathcal{S}}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x;\theta)}\left[\cdot\right]\,,
𝔼𝒮[⋅|𝒵]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}}\left[\cdot\,\middle|\,\mathcal{Z}\right] =𝔼τ𝒮∼π(⋅∣x;θ)[⋅|x,τ𝒵].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{\mathcal{S}}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x;\theta)}\left[\cdot\,\middle|\,x,\tau_{\mathcal{Z}}\right]\,.

Here 𝔼𝒮​[⋅]\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}}\left[\cdot\right] is the expectation over actions and observations at steps 𝒮\mathcal{S}, and context xx; and 𝔼𝒮[⋅|𝒵]\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}}\left[\cdot\,\middle|\,\mathcal{Z}\right] is the expectation over actions and observations at steps 𝒮\mathcal{S}, conditioned on actions and observations at steps 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, and context xx. With the new notation in hand, we get the following claim.

Lemma 2.

Let x∼qx\sim q and τn∼π(⋅∣x;θ)\tau_{n}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x;\theta). Then for any ℛt⊆[n]∖[t−1]\mathcal{R}_{t}\subseteq[n]\setminus[t-1], the gradient in (5) is equal to

𝔼⁡[∑t=1n∇𝔼𝒮t​[rt|𝒮¯t]].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{n}\nabla\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}\left[r_{t}\,\middle|\,\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\right]\right]\,.

The proof is in Section A.3. The lemma says that the gradient in (5) increases the sum of expected per-step rewards rtr_{t} through actions at steps 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} that affect the corresponding expected rewards. The histories 𝒮¯t\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t} are sampled from π\pi. We discuss different forms of these policies in Section 4.

3.4 Offline Partial Policy Gradient

So far, we focused on online policy gradients (Section 3.2), where the trajectories are sampled from learned policy π\pi. Another common and practical setting is offline RL (Jaques et al., 2020; Levine et al., 2020), where the trajectories are sampled from a logged dataset. We represent it by another distribution ρ\rho and propose an offline partial policy gradient of the form

𝔼ρ[∑t=1n(∑ℓ∈ℛtrℓ)∇logπ(at∣x,τt−1;θ)],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{\rho}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{R}_{t}}r_{\ell}\right)\nabla\log\pi(a_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1};\theta)\right]\,, (8)

where 𝔼ρ[⋅]=𝔼x∼q,τn∼ρ(⋅∣x;θ)[⋅]\mathbb{E}^{\rho}\left[\cdot\right]=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim q,\,\tau_{n}\sim\rho(\cdot\mid x;\theta)}\left[\cdot\right]. Note that the only difference from (5) is that the trajectories are sampled from another policy ρ\rho. Therefore, the empirical estimator of (8) from batch ℬ\mathcal{B} has the same algebraic form as (6).

Based on our discussion, an offline variant of 𝙿𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPG can be obtained by changing the sampling distribution in Line 7 of Algorithm 1 to τi,n∼ρ(⋅∣x;θ)\tau_{i,n}\sim\rho(\cdot\mid x;\theta). Our gradient estimator is motivated by Mukherjee et al. (2025) and can be related to maximizing the original online objective as follows.

Lemma 3.

Let all quantities be defined as in Lemma 2. Let 𝔼ρ\mathbb{E}^{\rho} be an expectation with respect to another policy ρ\rho. Then for any ℛt⊆[n]∖[t−1]\mathcal{R}_{t}\subseteq[n]\setminus[t-1], the gradient in (8) is equal to

𝔼ρ​[∑t=1n∇𝔼𝒮tρ[rt∑ℓ∈𝒮tlogπ(aℓ,yℓ∣x,τℓ−1;θ)|𝒮¯t]⏟ft​(θ)].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{\rho}\Bigg[\sum_{t=1}^{n}\nabla\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}^{\rho}\left[r_{t}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\log\pi(a_{\ell},y_{\ell}\mid x,\tau_{\ell-1};\theta)\,\middle|\,\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\right]}_{f_{t}(\theta)}\Bigg]\,.

When rt≥0r_{t}\geq 0 for all t∈[n]t\in[n], ft​(θ)≤𝔼𝒮t​[rt|𝒮¯t]f_{t}(\theta)\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}\left[r_{t}\,\middle|\,\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\right] holds. In general, |ft​(θ)−𝔼𝒮t​[rt|𝒮¯t]|≤C⁡(π,ρ)|f_{t}(\theta)-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}\left[r_{t}\,\middle|\,\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\right]|\leq C(\pi,\rho), where C⁡(π,ρ)C(\pi,\rho) is a constant depending on the propensity ratios of π\pi and ρ\rho, and their logarithms.

The proof is in Section A.4. The first claim says that the gradient increases the sum of expected per-step rewards rtr_{t} weighted by log-probabilities under logging policy ρ\rho, denoted by ft​(θ)f_{t}(\theta), through actions at steps 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} that affect them. The second claim says that the true objective 𝔼𝒮t​[rt|𝒮¯t]\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}\left[r_{t}\,\middle|\,\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\right] that we want to optimize is bounded from below by ft​(θ)f_{t}(\theta), which we optimize. The lower bound holds under the assumption that rt≥0r_{t}\geq 0. Without it, ft​(θ)f_{t}(\theta) is still C⁡(π,ρ)C(\pi,\rho) close to 𝔼𝒮t​[rt|𝒮¯t]\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}\left[r_{t}\,\middle|\,\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\right], as stated in the last claim.

Since Lemma 3 provides guarantees for negative rewards, offline 𝙿𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPG can be implemented with advantages and we do that in Section 5. The advantage for step tt in trajectory ii is computed as

r~i,t=∑ℓ∈ℛtri,ℓ−μ𝒢σ𝒢,\displaystyle\tilde{r}_{i,t}=\frac{\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{R}_{t}}r_{i,\ell}-\mu_{\mathcal{G}}}{\sigma_{\mathcal{G}}}\,, (9)

where μ𝒢\mu_{\mathcal{G}} and σ𝒢\sigma_{\mathcal{G}} are the mean and standard deviation of ∑ℓ∈ℛtrj,ℓ\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{R}_{t}}r_{j,\ell} computed jointly over j∈𝒢j\in\mathcal{G} and t∈[n]t\in[n], where 𝒢\mathcal{G} is the group of trajectories that trajectory ii belongs to. In our experiments in Section 5, we group the trajectories by the persona and topic.

4 Partial Policy Gradient Instances

To show the generality of our framework, we derive and compare several instances of 𝙿𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPG. Our concentration arguments rely on Theorem 5, which is stated and proved in Section A.2. Segment policies are derived in Section A.5. Offline policy gradients can be derived analogously.

4.1 Full Policy Gradient

Suppose that all actions ata_{t} in (5) affect all future rewards. Then ℛt=[n]∖[t−1]\mathcal{R}_{t}=[n]\setminus[t-1] for all steps t∈[n]t\in[n]. By Lemma 2, where 𝒮t=[t]\mathcal{S}_{t}=[t] and 𝒮¯t=∅\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}=\emptyset, the gradient is

𝔼⁡[∑t=1n∇𝔼[t]​[rt]]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{n}\nabla\mathbb{E}_{[t]}\left[r_{t}\right]\right] =𝔼[∇∑t=1n𝔼[t][rt]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\nabla\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{[t]}\left[r_{t}\right]\right] (10)
=𝔼⁡[∇𝔼​[∑t=1nrt]]=∇𝔼​[r].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\nabla\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{n}r_{t}\right]\right]=\nabla\mathbb{E}\left[r\right]\,.

In plain English, all actions up to step tt affect the reward at step tt; and the gradient is a sum of gradients of the corresponding expected rewards. Note that it is identical to (2), because future actions do not affect past rewards.

4.2 Greedy Policy Gradient

Suppose that all actions ata_{t} in (5) affect only the immediate reward. Then ℛt={t}\mathcal{R}_{t}=\left\{t\right\} for all t∈[n]t\in[n]. By Lemma 2, where 𝒮t={t}\mathcal{S}_{t}=\left\{t\right\} and 𝒮¯t=[t−1]\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}=[t-1], the gradient is

𝔼⁡[∑t=1n∇𝔼{t}​[rt|[t−1]]].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{n}\nabla\mathbb{E}_{\left\{t\right\}}\left[r_{t}\,\middle|\,[t-1]\right]\right]\,. (11)

In plain English, only the action at step tt affects the reward at step tt; and the gradient is a sum of gradients of the corresponding expected rewards. We refer to 𝙿𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPG with ℛt={t}\mathcal{R}_{t}=\left\{t\right\} as 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG.

This policy is simpler than that in Section 4.1, where the reward is affected by each previous action, and therefore its gradient can be estimated more efficiently. Specifically, by Theorem 5, the empirical gradient in 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG concentrates faster than that in 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG since 𝒮t={t}⊆[t]\mathcal{S}_{t}=\left\{t\right\}\subseteq[t]. While this policy class was proposed, analyzed, and evaluated in LLMs by Kveton et al. (2025), it was done only for adaptive submodular maximization (Golovin and Krause, 2011). The connection to statistical efficiency was not established.

4.3 KK-Step Lookahead Policy Gradient

Suppose that all actions ata_{t} in (5) affect the next KK rewards. Then ℛt=[min⁡{t+K−1,n}]∖[t−1]\mathcal{R}_{t}=[\min\left\{t+K-1,n\right\}]\setminus[t-1] for all t∈[n]t\in[n]. By Lemma 2, where 𝒮t=[t]∖[max⁡{t−K,0}]\mathcal{S}_{t}=[t]\setminus[\max\left\{t-K,0\right\}] and 𝒮¯t=[max⁡{t−K,0}]\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}=[\max\left\{t-K,0\right\}], the gradient is

𝔼⁡[∑t=1n∇𝔼[t]∖[max⁡{t−K,0}]​[rt|[max⁡{t−K,0}]]].\displaystyle\!\!\!\!\!\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{n}\nabla\mathbb{E}_{[t]\setminus[\max\left\{t-K,0\right\}]}\left[r_{t}\,\middle|\,[\max\left\{t-K,0\right\}]\right]\right]\,. (12)

In plain English, only the last KK actions up to step tt including affect the reward at step tt; and the gradient is a sum of gradients of the corresponding expected rewards. We call 𝙿𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPG with this ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} as 𝙺−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt K\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG. Our paper is the first work that proposes this policy in LLMs. For a given lookahead, such as K=3K=3, we write 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG. Note that 𝟷−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 1\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG is identical to 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG in Section 4.2.

This policy is simpler than that in Section 4.1, where the reward is affected by each previous action, but also more complex than that in Section 4.2, where the reward is affected only by the immediate action. The policy naturally interpolates between these two extremes. Specifically, since

{t}⊆𝒮t=[t]∖[max⁡{t−K,0}]⊆[t]\displaystyle\left\{t\right\}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{t}=[t]\setminus[\max\left\{t-K,0\right\}]\subseteq[t]

holds for any KK, we have by Theorem 5 that the empirical gradient in 𝙺−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt K\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG concentrates faster than that in 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG but slower than that in 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG. The complexity of the policy increases and its concentration rate decreases as KK increases.

5 Experiments

We describe our benchmarks in Section 5.1, evaluation protocol in Section 5.2, and baselines in Section 5.3. The policies are evaluated in Section 5.4. We analyze their stability in Section 5.5 and statistical efficiency in Section 5.6. In addition, we study the policies across conversation lengths in Appendix C, present scaling laws for Qwen, Llama, and Gemma models in generic domain in Appendix B, and give qualitative examples in Appendix G.

5.1 Data Settings

Problem Formulation. Our learning problem is maintaining consistent and faithful human personas over time in role-playing dialogues like therapy, education, and chatting. We instantiate the framework in Section 2 as follows. The context xx is a persona definition given at the start of the interaction in a system prompt. A trajectory τn\tau_{n} is a dialogue history between an LLM-simulated agent and the environment. The agent’s responses are actions ata_{t} and the environment’s replies are observations yty_{t}.

Dataset. We experiment with Consistent-LLMs benchmark (Abdulhai et al., 2025), which provides human-persona dialogues across 3 distinct domains: (i) Education: Tutoring sessions where a student agent maintains specific learning preferences and the tutor acts as the environment; (ii) Therapy: Counseling sessions where a patient agent maintains consistent mental health backgrounds while the therapist serves as the environment; and (iii) Chatting: Casual dialogue where a simulated human is the agent maintaining biographical consistency (family, career, and so on) against a conversational environment. Each domain comprises of 6 5006\,500 trajectories (5 2005\,200 training and 1 3001\,300 test) of varying lengths (22 to 6060 steps, with 2323 steps on average). The trajectories are generated using a Llama-3.1-8B model.

5.2 Evaluation

Abdulhai et al. (2025) proposed two metrics to evaluate role-playing consistency: (i) Prompt consistency measures if an agent’s response aligns with their assigned persona or background. (ii) Index consistency evaluates if an agent’s response contradicts to their own previous responses in the conversation history based on their past prompt consistency scores. Since index consistency is a secondary metric derived from prompt consistency, we use prompt consistency in our work; and call it persona consistency (PC) because it measures the consistency of a persona. Using this terminology, the reward at step tt, rt=r⁡(x,τt)r_{t}=r(x,\tau_{t}), is its PC.

All policies are learned offline from the training trajectories of Abdulhai et al. (2025). At test time, we measure the PC using an LLM judge with the same prompts as in Abdulhai et al. (2025). Specifically, for each agent’s response ata_{t}, we ask the LLM judge to evaluate if it contradicts the persona description provided as context xx and score it 11 (consistent) if the judge outputs “NO” (no contradiction) or 00 (inconsistent) if the judge outputs “YES” (contradiction detected). The judge is implemented using GPT-4o mini with temperature 00, and we report the mean scores across all steps of the evaluated trajectories. See prompts in Appendix E.

We employ two complementary evaluation protocols to assess persona consistency under different distribution conditions. The first follows the rollout methodology from Abdulhai et al. (2025), while the second is designed to isolate consistency improvements from error propagation effects.

Rollout evaluation. Following Abdulhai et al. (2025), we generate complete conversation trajectories starting with only the initial persona description as context, alternating between responses of the agent and a fixed simulated environment implemented using Llama-3.1-70B model. This exposes the agent to distribution shifts, as inconsistencies compound over time, making it a challenging test of maintaining long-horizon consistency.

Step-level evaluation. To disentangle consistency improvements from error compounding, we introduce a controlled evaluation setting where each step is assessed independently. Specifically, we take the test trajectories of Abdulhai et al. (2025) and for each step in them, we generate the response of the agent given the conversation history of that particular trajectory. This design isolates the model’s inherent consistency capability from the cascading effects of its own errors without model-induced distribution shift.

5.3 Baselines and Compared Methods

We have two baselines. 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base is an unmodified base model used zero-shot to show what can be attained without learning. PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) was used as a policy optimization algorithm in Abdulhai et al. (2025), and hence is a state-of-the-art baseline in our domain. We experiment with two agent models: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B, which we abbreviate as Qwen and Llama, respectively.

All our policies are learned offline by an offline policy gradient (Section 3.4), where ρ\rho samples trajectories uniformly at random from the training set. The reward at step tt is the persona consistency at step tt (Section 5.2). The rewards are standardized as in (9). We learn a full planning policy (𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG in Section 4.1), greedy policy (𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG in Section 4.2), and KK-step lookahead policies (𝙺−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt K\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG in Section 4.3) for K={2,3,4,5}K=\{2,3,4,5\}. Additional training details in Appendix F.

5.4 Main Results

We start by evaluating all policies in all domains: education, therapy, and chatting; and report their average persona consistency in Tables 1, 2 and 3. While the best performing policy is domain-dependent, policy gradients universally outperform 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base and PPO, demonstrating the robustness of offline RL by policy gradients. In chatting and therapy domains, KK-step lookahead policies (𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG and 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG) perform extremely well across both Qwen and Llama models. 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG is the best policy in the education domain, because a faithful simulation of a tutored student requires long-term planning. We observe consistent results across rollout and step-level evaluation methodologies, suggesting that our gains are robust despite the cascading errors commonly observed in long dialogues. Our results show similar trends for both Qwen and Llama models, suggesting that our approach generalizes across multiple LLM architectures.

5.5 On Effectiveness of Simpler Policies

Now we try to understand the best performing policies. For all policies, we compute the mean persona consistency at each conversation step, subtract the mean over all steps, and renormalize to [−1,1][-1,1] jointly over all policies. Note that this is just a linear transformation of consistency scores that makes them comparable across the policies. We call this quantity a residual and report it in Figure 2. The residual of 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base monotonically decreases as conversation progresses, confirming that LLMs are susceptible to persona drift in long-horizon conversations (Nie et al., 2021). The residual of 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG oscillates a lot. These ripples reflect the policy’s repeated failed recovery attempts from persona drift, due to not planning for the future. In comparison, KK-step lookahead policies (𝙺−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt K\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG) maintain stable residuals across trajectory steps. We observe that increasing KK from K=1K=1 (𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG) to K=3K=3 (𝙺−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt K\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG) produces progressively smoother residuals, supporting our theory that assigning credit to longer horizons can prevent persona drift by maintaining consistency continuously over time. Finally, in therapy and chatting domains, we observe that 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG oscillates a lot and thus performs worse than 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG. This experiment shows that the temporal scope of credit assignment directly influences policy stability, with longer horizons providing smoother and more robust behavior at the cost of increased data requirements. Results for Llama are in Appendix D. See qualitative analysis in Appendix G.

5.6 On Statistical Efficiency of Simpler Policies

We investigate the statistical efficiency of learning different policies next. Specifically, we vary the number of training trajectories, from 5050 (low-data regime, 1%1\% of training data) to 5 0005\,000 (high-data regime, all training data), and plot the persona consistency of all policies in Figure 3. Our results reveal a fundamental trade-off between policy complexity and statistical efficiency. In the low-data regime, 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG consistently excels in all domains, confirming our hypothesis that simpler policies are easier to learn when data are scarce. As data scales to moderate levels (500500 trajectories, 10%10\% of training data), KK-step lookahead policies dominate across all domains. In particular, 𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG and 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG are the best policies in therapy and chatting domains. These policies strike balance between planning enough for the future and being able to learn it. In the education domain, we observe that full planning with 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG eventually achieves the highest persona consistency in the high-data regime. We validate this scaling behavior across three model architectures (Llama, Qwen, Gemma) on an additional dataset (Synthetic Persona Chat  (Jandaghi et al., 2024)) in Appendix B, confirming that optimal lookahead horizon KK consistently increases with available training data, establishing a practical design principle for calibrating policy complexity to data budgets.

6 Related Work

The closest related works are Kveton et al. (2025) and Guo et al. (2025). Kveton et al. (2025) optimized greedy policies using online policy gradients and Guo et al. (2025) optimized segment policies using GRPO. Our formalism captures both of these policy classes. Unlike Kveton et al. (2025), we consider more general optimization problems than adaptive submodularity (Golovin and Krause, 2011). Unlike Guo et al. (2025), we consider a general RL model that allows observations of the environment.

Learning of policies in finite-horizon Markov decision processes is a classic topic and it is well known that they are non-stationary (Puterman, 1994). Monte Carlo estimation of Q values, by the sum of infinite-horizon discounted rewards, is discussed in detail in Sutton and Barto (1998) and was generalized to advantages by Schulman et al. (2016). We do not discount rewards and show that maximization of a subset of future rewards results in a new simpler policy that is easier to learn. KK-step lookahead policies were studied in other contexts before. Efroni et al. (2018a) used them to improve policy iteration, Efroni et al. (2018b) applied them to online and approximate RL, and Efroni et al. (2020) extended them to real-time dynamic programming. Adaptive lookahead polices were studied by Rosenberg et al. (2023) and KK-step lookahead policies were used in offline RL by Sikchi et al. (2022). The main difference in our work is that we only use policy gradients without any additional model, such as that of a value or Q function.

7 Conclusions

Most popular RL algorithms in LLMs are variants of policy gradients. In this work, we propose a natural approach for introducing policy structure in policy gradients. The key idea is to optimize for a subset of future rewards. Smaller subsets of rewards define simpler policies, which can be learned more reliably because their empirical gradients are more accurate. We interpret the policies, and propose both online and offline algorithms for learning them. Full planning, greedy, KK-step lookahead, and segment policies are all instances of our framework. We evaluate the policies on conversation optimization problems and observe that different policies excel in different domains, highlighting the importance of our introduced structure. We note that the idea of optimizing for subsets of future rewards is general and can be straightforwardly applied to regularized policies (Todorov, 2006) and also GRPO (Shao et al., 2024).

Limitations. First, our work provides both theory and experiments that justify policy optimization for subsets of future rewards. However, we never formally show that the better performance in our experiments is due to a lower variance in policy gradient estimates. Second, the per-step reward in (4) is an important design choice that may have impact on empirical performance. We do not ablate it and instead rely on existing works to provide it (Section 5). Finally, our evaluation is limited to conversational problems, although we experiment with four different problems and three LLMs.

Impact Statement

This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.
