Appendix A Additional Technical Contributions

This section contains proofs of our main claims and supporting lemmas.

A.1 Proof of Lemma 1

The proof is based on telescoping,

∑t=1nrt=∑t=1nf⁡(x,τt)−f⁡(x,τt−1)=f⁡(x,τn)−f⁡(x,τ0)=r⁡(x,τn).\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{n}r_{t}=\sum_{t=1}^{n}f(x,\tau_{t})-f(x,\tau_{t-1})=f(x,\tau_{n})-f(x,\tau_{0})=r(x,\tau_{n})\,.

The rewards rtr_{t} are non-negative because ff is monotone.

A.2 Gradient Concentration

The main tool used in our analysis is Hoeffding’s inequality [Raginsky and Sason, 2012, Boucheron et al., 2013], which we restate below for completeness.

Theorem 4.

Let X1,…,XnX_{1},\dots,X_{n} be nn independent random variables such that Xi∈[−ci,ci]X_{i}\in[-c_{i},c_{i}] holds almost surely for some ci>0c_{i}>0. Then for any ε>0\varepsilon>0,

ℙ⁡(|X1+⋯+Xn−𝔼⁡[X1+⋯+Xn]|≥ε)≤2​exp⁡[−ε22​∑i=1nci2].\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(|X_{1}+\dots+X_{n}-\mathbb{E}\left[X_{1}+\dots+X_{n}\right]|\geq\varepsilon\right)\leq 2\exp\left[-\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}^{2}}\right]\,.

We state our main theorem next.

Theorem 5.

Let g⁡(ℬ)g(\mathcal{B}) and g′​(ℬ)g^{\prime}(\mathcal{B}) be partial policy gradient estimators such that 𝒮t⊆𝒮t′\mathcal{S}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{S}^{\prime}_{t} holds for all t∈[n]t\in[n], where 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} and 𝒮t′\mathcal{S}^{\prime}_{t} are their action indices that affect the reward at step tt. Then g⁡(ℬ)g(\mathcal{B}) concentrates in the 22-norm faster than g′​(ℬ)g^{\prime}(\mathcal{B}).

Proof.

We apply Hoeffding’s inequality as follows. Let

f(ℬ)=∑i=1B∑t=1n∑ℓ∈𝒮tri,t∇logπ(ai,ℓ∣xi,τi,ℓ−1;θ),\displaystyle f(\mathcal{B})=\sum_{i=1}^{B}\sum_{t=1}^{n}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}r_{i,t}\nabla\log\pi(a_{i,\ell}\mid x_{i},\tau_{i,\ell-1};\theta)\,, (13)

where ℬ\mathcal{B} is the batch in Algorithm 1 and 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} is the set of action indices that affect the reward at step tt (Section 3.3). Note that f⁡(ℬ)f(\mathcal{B}) is a dd-dimensional vector, where dd is the number of policy parameters θ\theta with respect to which the gradient is taken. For any j∈[d]j\in[d], let fj​(ℬ)f_{j}(\mathcal{B}) be the jj-th entry of f⁡(ℬ)f(\mathcal{B}).

Because of the identity in (7), we have f⁡(ℬ)=B​g​(ℬ)f(\mathcal{B})=Bg(\mathcal{B}). Using norm identities and the union bound, we get

ℙ⁡(‖g⁡(ℬ)−𝔼⁡[g⁡(ℬ)]‖2≥ε)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\|g(\mathcal{B})-\mathbb{E}\left[g(\mathcal{B})\right]\|_{2}\geq\varepsilon\right) =ℙ⁡(‖f⁡(ℬ)−𝔼⁡[f⁡(ℬ)]‖2≥ε​B)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\|f(\mathcal{B})-\mathbb{E}\left[f(\mathcal{B})\right]\|_{2}\geq\varepsilon B\right)
≤ℙ⁡(d​maxj∈[d]​|fj​(ℬ)−𝔼⁡[fj​(ℬ)]|≥ε​B)\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\sqrt{d}\max_{j\in[d]}|f_{j}(\mathcal{B})-\mathbb{E}\left[f_{j}(\mathcal{B})\right]|\geq\varepsilon B\right)
≤∑j=1dℙ⁡(|fj​(ℬ)−𝔼⁡[fj​(ℬ)]|≥ε​Bd).\displaystyle\leq\sum_{j=1}^{d}\mathbb{P}\left(|f_{j}(\mathcal{B})-\mathbb{E}\left[f_{j}(\mathcal{B})\right]|\geq\frac{\varepsilon B}{\sqrt{d}}\right)\,.

Now note that fj​(ℬ)f_{j}(\mathcal{B}) is a sum of B​∑t=1n|𝒮t|B\sum_{t=1}^{n}|\mathcal{S}_{t}| random scalars but 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} is fixed. Let |ri,t​(∇log⁡π​(ai,ℓ∣xi,τi,ℓ−1;θ))j|≤ct,ℓ|r_{i,t}(\nabla\log\pi(a_{i,\ell}\mid x_{i},\tau_{i,\ell-1};\theta))_{j}|\leq c_{t,\ell} hold almost surely and jointly for all i∈[B]i\in[B] and j∈[d]j\in[d]. Then, since the vectors in (13) can be arbitrarily correlated,

|∑t=1n∑ℓ∈𝒮tri,t​(∇log⁡π​(ai,ℓ∣xi,τi,ℓ−1;θ))j|≤∑t=1n∑ℓ∈𝒮tct,ℓ\displaystyle\left|\sum_{t=1}^{n}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}r_{i,t}(\nabla\log\pi(a_{i,\ell}\mid x_{i},\tau_{i,\ell-1};\theta))_{j}\right|\leq\sum_{t=1}^{n}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}c_{t,\ell}

holds almost surely and jointly for all i∈[B]i\in[B] and j∈[d]j\in[d]. So by Theorem 4, for any j∈[d]j\in[d] and ε>0\varepsilon>0,

ℙ⁡(|fj​(ℬ)−𝔼⁡[fj​(ℬ)]|≥ε​Bd)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(|f_{j}(\mathcal{B})-\mathbb{E}\left[f_{j}(\mathcal{B})\right]|\geq\frac{\varepsilon B}{\sqrt{d}}\right) ≤2​exp⁡[−ε2​B22​d​B​(∑t=1n∑ℓ∈𝒮tct,ℓ)2]\displaystyle\leq 2\exp\left[-\frac{\varepsilon^{2}B^{2}}{2dB\left(\sum_{t=1}^{n}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}c_{t,\ell}\right)^{2}}\right]
≤2​exp⁡[−ε2​B2​d​(∑t=1n∑ℓ∈𝒮tct,ℓ)2].\displaystyle\leq 2\exp\left[-\frac{\varepsilon^{2}B}{2d\left(\sum_{t=1}^{n}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}c_{t,\ell}\right)^{2}}\right]\,.

Finally, we chain all inequalities and get

ℙ⁡(‖g⁡(ℬ)−𝔼⁡[g⁡(ℬ)]‖2≥ε)≤2​d​exp​[−ε2​B2​d​(∑t=1n∑ℓ∈𝒮tct,ℓ)2].\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\|g(\mathcal{B})-\mathbb{E}\left[g(\mathcal{B})\right]\|_{2}\geq\varepsilon\right)\leq 2d\exp\left[-\frac{\varepsilon^{2}B}{2d\left(\sum_{t=1}^{n}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}c_{t,\ell}\right)^{2}}\right]\,.

The bound shows that the concentration rate decreases as ∑t=1n∑ℓ∈𝒮tct,ℓ\sum_{t=1}^{n}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}c_{t,\ell} increases. Therefore, for any two partial policy gradient estimators g⁡(ℬ)g(\mathcal{B}) and g′​(ℬ)g^{\prime}(\mathcal{B}) such that 𝒮t⊆𝒮t′\mathcal{S}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{S}^{\prime}_{t} for all t∈[n]t\in[n], the former concentrates faster than the latter in the worst case. ∎

A.3 Proof of Lemma 2

Using rules of probability,

𝔼[∑t=1n(∑ℓ∈ℛtrℓ)∇logπ(at∣x,τt−1;θ)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{R}_{t}}r_{\ell}\right)\nabla\log\pi(a_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1};\theta)\right] =𝔼⁡[∑t=1nrt​∑ℓ∈𝒮t∇log⁡π​(aℓ∣x,τℓ−1;θ)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{n}r_{t}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\nabla\log\pi(a_{\ell}\mid x,\tau_{\ell-1};\theta)\right]
=∑t=1n𝔼⁡[rt​∑ℓ∈𝒮t∇log⁡π​(aℓ∣x,τℓ−1;θ)]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[r_{t}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\nabla\log\pi(a_{\ell}\mid x,\tau_{\ell-1};\theta)\right]
=∑t=1n𝔼𝒮¯t​[𝔼𝒮t​[rt​∑ℓ∈𝒮t∇log⁡π​(aℓ∣x,τℓ−1;θ)|𝒮¯t]]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}\left[r_{t}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\nabla\log\pi(a_{\ell}\mid x,\tau_{\ell-1};\theta)\,\middle|\,\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\right]\right]
=∑t=1n𝔼𝒮¯t​[∇𝔼𝒮t​[rt|𝒮¯t]]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}}\left[\nabla\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}\left[r_{t}\,\middle|\,\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\right]\right]
=𝔼⁡[∑t=1n∇𝔼𝒮t​[rt|𝒮¯t]].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{n}\nabla\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}\left[r_{t}\,\middle|\,\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\right]\right]\,.

We apply (7) in the first step, the linearity of expectation in the second step, the tower rule in the third step, the score identity over random τ𝒮t\tau_{\mathcal{S}_{t}} in the fourth step, and the tower rule in the last step. This completes the proof.

A.4 Proof of Lemma 3

Using the tower rule and that ρ\rho does not depend on the differentiated θ\theta, we get

𝔼ρ[∑t=1n(∑ℓ∈ℛtrℓ)∇logπ(at∣x,τt−1;θ)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{\rho}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{R}_{t}}r_{\ell}\right)\nabla\log\pi(a_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1};\theta)\right] =𝔼ρ​[∑t=1nrt​∑ℓ∈𝒮t∇log⁡π​(aℓ∣x,τℓ−1;θ)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}^{\rho}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{n}r_{t}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\nabla\log\pi(a_{\ell}\mid x,\tau_{\ell-1};\theta)\right]
=∑t=1n𝔼ρ​[rt​∑ℓ∈𝒮t∇log⁡π​(aℓ∣x,τℓ−1;θ)]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}^{\rho}\left[r_{t}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\nabla\log\pi(a_{\ell}\mid x,\tau_{\ell-1};\theta)\right]
=∑t=1n𝔼𝒮¯tρ​[𝔼𝒮tρ​[rt​∑ℓ∈𝒮t∇log⁡π​(aℓ∣x,τℓ−1;θ)|𝒮¯t]]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}}^{\rho}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}^{\rho}\left[r_{t}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\nabla\log\pi(a_{\ell}\mid x,\tau_{\ell-1};\theta)\,\middle|\,\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\right]\right]
=∑t=1n𝔼𝒮¯tρ[∇𝔼𝒮tρ[rt∑ℓ∈𝒮tlogπ(aℓ,yℓ∣x,τℓ−1;θ)|𝒮¯t]]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}}^{\rho}\left[\nabla\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}^{\rho}\left[r_{t}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\log\pi(a_{\ell},y_{\ell}\mid x,\tau_{\ell-1};\theta)\,\middle|\,\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\right]\right]
=𝔼ρ[∑t=1n∇𝔼𝒮tρ[rt∑ℓ∈𝒮tlogπ(aℓ,yℓ∣x,τℓ−1;θ)|𝒮¯t]].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}^{\rho}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{n}\nabla\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}^{\rho}\left[r_{t}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}_{t}}\log\pi(a_{\ell},y_{\ell}\mid x,\tau_{\ell-1};\theta)\,\middle|\,\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\right]\right]\,.

The inequality

𝔼𝒮tρ[rt∑ℓ∈Stlogπ(at,yt∣x,τt−1;θ)|𝒮¯t]≤𝔼𝒮t[rt|𝒮¯t]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}^{\rho}\left[r_{t}\sum_{\ell\in S_{t}}\log\pi(a_{t},y_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1};\theta)\,\middle|\,\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\right]\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}\left[r_{t}\,\middle|\,\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\right]

follows from Lemma 1 of Mukherjee et al. [2025]. The only difference is that the expectation is taken over steps 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} of the trajectory conditioned on 𝒮¯t=[t]∖𝒮t\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}=[t]\setminus\mathcal{S}_{t}, which does not change the proof.

Similarly, the bound

|𝔼𝒮tρ[rt∑ℓ∈Stlogπ(at,yt∣x,τt−1;θ)|𝒮¯t]−𝔼𝒮t[rt|𝒮¯t]|≤C(π,ρ),\displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}^{\rho}\left[r_{t}\sum_{\ell\in S_{t}}\log\pi(a_{t},y_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1};\theta)\,\middle|\,\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}_{t}}\left[r_{t}\,\middle|\,\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}\right]\right|\leq C(\pi,\rho)\,,

follows from Lemma 3 of Mukherjee et al. [2025], where C⁡(π,ρ)C(\pi,\rho) is a constant depending on the propensity ratios of π\pi and ρ\rho, and their logarithms. The only difference is that the expectation is taken over steps 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} of the trajectory conditioned on 𝒮¯t=[t]∖𝒮t\bar{\mathcal{S}}_{t}=[t]\setminus\mathcal{S}_{t}, which does not change the proof.

A.5 KK-Segment Policy Gradient

Let 𝒞1,…,𝒞K⊂[n]\mathcal{C}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{C}_{K}\subset[n] be sets of consecutive step indices representing segments, which are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Let mk=min⁡𝒞km_{k}=\min\mathcal{C}_{k} and Mk=max⁡𝒞kM_{k}=\max\mathcal{C}_{k} be the minimum and maximum indices within segment CkC_{k}. Let ktk_{t} be the segment of step tt. Then 𝒮t=[t]∖[mkt−1]\mathcal{S}_{t}=[t]\setminus[m_{k_{t}}-1] are the future rewards in segment CktC_{k_{t}} starting from step tt. By Lemma 2, where 𝒮t=[t]∖[mkt−1]\mathcal{S}_{t}=[t]\setminus[m_{k_{t}}-1], the gradient is

𝔼⁡[∑k=1K∑t∈𝒞k∇𝔼[t]∖[mkt−1]​[rt|[mkt−1]]]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\nabla\mathbb{E}_{[t]\setminus[m_{k_{t}}-1]}\left[r_{t}\,\middle|\,[m_{k_{t}}-1]\right]\right] (14)
=𝔼⁡[∑k=1K∇𝔼​[∑t∈𝒞krt|[mkt−1]]].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{K}\nabla\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}r_{t}\,\middle|\,[m_{k_{t}}-1]\right]\right]\,.

In plain English, all actions up to step tt within its segment CktC_{k_{t}} affect the reward at step tt; and the gradient is a sum of gradients of the corresponding expected rewards. We refer to 𝙿𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPG with this ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} as 𝙺−𝚂𝚎𝚐−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt K\mathchar 45\relax Seg\mathchar 45\relax PG. This policy class was proposed in LLMs by Guo et al. [2025].

This policy is simpler than that in Section 4.1, where the reward is affected by each previous action, but also more complex than that in Section 4.2, where the reward is affected only by the immediate action. As in Section 4.3, the policy naturally interpolates between these two extremes. Since

{t}⊆𝒮t=[t]∖[mkt−1]⊆[t]\displaystyle\left\{t\right\}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{t}=[t]\setminus[m_{k_{t}}-1]\subseteq[t]

holds for any segments 𝒞1,…,𝒞K\mathcal{C}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{C}_{K}, we have by Theorem 5 that the empirical gradient in 𝙺−𝚂𝚎𝚐−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt K\mathchar 45\relax Seg\mathchar 45\relax PG concentrates faster than that in 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG but slower than that in 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG. The rate depends on the size of the segments.

Appendix B Scaling Laws for Partial Policy Gradients

Motivation. In Figure 3, we demonstrated that simpler policies (𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG) exhibit superior statistical efficiency in low-data regimes compared to complex policies (𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG), with the performance gap narrowing as training data increases. This raises a practical question: how does the optimal lookahead horizon K scale with available training data across different model architectures? Understanding this scaling relationship is critical for practitioners who must choose appropriate credit assignment horizons given their data budget constraints.

Experimental Design. To investigate this scaling behavior systematically, we replicate the statistical efficiency experiment from the main paper using a complementary dataset: the Synthetic Persona Chat dataset [Jandaghi et al., 2024], which contains generic and mixed-domain personas distinct from our primary Education, Therapy, and Chatting domains. We sample 20,000 trajectories from this dataset and train all policy variants (𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base, 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG, 𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG, 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG, 𝟺−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 4\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG, 𝟻−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 5\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG, 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG) with varying amounts of training data, ranging from 100 to 20,000 trajectories. For each data size, we measure which policy achieves the best persona consistency on a held-out test set. We repeat this procedure across three different LLM architectures—Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen-2.5-7B, and Gemma-7B-it—to assess whether the scaling laws are architecture-dependent or represent a general phenomenon.

Observation. Figure 4 shows the optimal policy (represented by its lookahead horizon K on the y-axis) as a function of available training trajectories (x-axis) for each model architecture. The key pattern is a consistent “staircase” structure: at low data regimes (50-1000 trajectories), 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base or 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG are optimal; as data increases to intermediate regimes (1000-5000 trajectories), 𝙺−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt K\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG with K=2,3,4 successively become optimal; and at high data regimes (>>10,000 trajectories), full planning (𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG) emerges as the best policy. Remarkably, this pattern holds across all three architectures, with only minor differences in the inflection points where transitions occur.

Interpretation. The results in Figure 4 demonstrate that the scaling behavior of KK-step lookahead policies is remarkably consistent across different model architectures. We observe a characteristic trend where the optimal complexity of the policy, represented by the lookahead KK, is a direct function of the available data volume. In low-data regimes, complex policies like full planning do not work effectively, and simpler objectives like 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG or low KK are preferred to achieve stable performance. However, as the number of trajectories increases beyond a critical threshold, higher-order policies become more effective, and full planning 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG eventually emerges as the best policy. This cross-architecture consistency validates our theoretical framework (Theorem 5): while simpler partial gradients concentrate faster, they optimize suboptimal policies, whereas complex policies require sufficient data to overcome higher variance in gradient estimation. These results establish a practical design principle for policy optimization in RL for LLMs: practitioners should calibrate policy complexity to available data, initializing with greedy policies in data-scarce regimes and progressively expanding the credit assignment horizon as data accumulates.

Appendix C Performance comparison of policy gradients across trajectory lengths

We provide a detailed analysis of how different policy gradient methods perform as a function of conversation length. While Tables 1, 2 and 3 report aggregate persona consistency (PC) across all trajectory lengths in the test set, here we disaggregate the results to examine performance trends as conversations become longer. This analysis reveals important insights about the stability of different credit assignment strategies over extended interactions.

Motivation. A critical question for persona-consistent LLMs is whether they can maintain consistency not just on average, but specifically in long conversations where persona drift is most problematic. Prior work has shown that base LLMs exhibit systematic degradation in longer dialogues [Nie et al., 2021, Abdulhai et al., 2025], but it remains unclear how different credit assignment horizons affect this degradation pattern.

Measurement. To investigate this, we partition our test trajectories by their length t∈{10,20,40,60}t\in\{10,20,40,60\} steps and compute the mean persona consistency scores separately for each length bin. We do this analysis only for the rollout evaluation setup. This measurement reveals whether policies maintain their performance advantages (or disadvantages) consistently across conversation lengths, or whether optimal policies differ for short vs. long conversations. Figures 5 and 6 present PC as a function of trajectory length for all compared policies across Education, Therapy, and Chatting domains, using Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B models respectively.

Baseline Degradation. The 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base policy exhibits monotonic degradation with conversation length across all three domains and both models. This validates the core motivation of our work: without proper temporal credit assignment, LLMs systematically lose persona consistency as conversations extend.

Domain-Specific Degradation Patterns. We observe that different domains exhibit distinct degradation characteristics. In the Education domain (Figure 5, left), 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base shows severe degradation, confirming that maintaining student personas over extended tutoring sessions is challenging without appropriate credit assignment. In contrast, 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG maintains remarkably stable performance validating that full planning is beneficial for education where long-term pedagogical strategies matter. In the Therapy domain, we observe that 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG achieves the most stable performance across conversation lengths for both models, showing that intermediate lookahead horizons balance consistency better than full planning in emotionally complex therapeutic contexts. In the Chatting domain, 𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG and 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG demonstrate exceptional stability, confirming that mid-step lookahead is particularly well-suited for casual conversations where planning too far ahead (𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG, 𝟻−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 5\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG) can actually degrade performance, especially in longer conversations.

Length-Dependent Policy Rankings. Importantly, we observe that optimal policy rankings are robust across trajectory lengths within each domain. For example, in Education, 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG consistently outperforms all other policies at every measured length (10, 20, 40, 60 steps). Similarly, in Chatting, 𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG maintains its dominance across all lengths. This robustness suggests that the domain-specific optimal credit assignment horizons identified in Section 5.4 are not artifacts of specific conversation lengths but reflect fundamental characteristics of each domain’s temporal structure.

Cross-Model Consistency. Comparing Figure 5 (Llama) and Figure 6 (Qwen), we observe that the relative policy rankings and degradation patterns are similar across architectures. For example, both models show 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG dominance in Education, 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG dominance in Therapy, and 𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG dominance in Chatting, with similar stability patterns across trajectory lengths. This cross-model consistency strengthens confidence that our findings about optimal credit assignment horizons reflect domain-specific requirements rather than model-specific artifacts.

Appendix D Stability of policy gradients for Llama3.1-8B model

We complement the stability analysis in Section 5.5 by presenting residual persona consistency plots for the Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model. While Figure 2 in the main text shows results for Qwen-2.5-7B, here we demonstrate that the stability patterns and policy behaviors generalize across different LLM architectures.

Residual Persona Consistency Metric. Following the methodology in Section 5.5, we compute residual PC for each policy as follows. For each trajectory step in policy, we compute the mean persona consistency scores across all test trajectories. We then subtract the overall mean consistency and renormalize to [−1,1][-1,1] jointly across all policies and steps. This linear transformation enables direct comparison of consistency patterns across policies by removing absolute performance differences and highlighting relative stability over conversation turns. Intuitively, policies with flat residuals (near zero throughout) maintain consistent performance across steps, while policies with oscillating or trending residuals exhibit instability or systematic drift.

Baseline Degradation. The 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base policy exhibits systematic negative drift across all three domains. This monotonic degradation confirms that base LLMs without credit-assignment-aware training suffer from accumulating persona drift in extended conversations, consistent with prior observations [Nie et al., 2021, Abdulhai et al., 2025].

Full Planning Oscillation. Interestingly, 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG shows low residuals early in conversations but exhibits occasionally in chatting and therapy domains. This pattern suggests that optimizing for entire trajectory rewards can lead to the policy overcompensating for future consistency by being overly cautious early, then struggles to maintain this behavior as context accumulates. This also explains why 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG underperforms shorter-horizon policies in Therapy and Chatting (Tables 2 and 3).

Greedy Oscillation. The 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG  displays significant oscillations across all domains, particularly in Therapy where residuals swing with multiple reversal points. These ”ripples” reflect the policy’s myopic nature: by only considering immediate rewards, 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG makes locally consistent decisions that create future inconsistencies, leading to repeated failed recovery attempts. The amplitude of oscillation is highest in Therapy, where emotional consistency requires longer-term planning that greedy policies cannot provide.

K-Step Stability. In stark contrast, intermediate lookahead policies (𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG, 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG) maintain remarkably flat residuals across trajectory steps. The stability improves monotonically from K=1 to K=3: comparing 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG (K=1), 𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG (K=2), and 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG (K=3) in Figure 7, we observe progressively smoother trajectories with reduced oscillation amplitude. This directly supports our theoretical motivation in Section 3: by assigning credit to appropriately-scoped future horizons, policies can anticipate and prevent consistency violations before they compound.

Cross-Model Validation. Comparing Figure 7 (Llama-3.1-8B) with Figure 2 (Qwen-2.5-7B) reveals strong qualitative agreement across architectures. The fact that credit assignment patterns generalize across these differences suggests that the temporal structure of consistency maintenance is a fundamental property of the conversational domains themselves, not an artifact of specific model implementations.

Appendix E Evaluation Prompts

This section provides the complete evaluation prompts used for consistency assessment with the LLM judge (gpt-4o-mini, temperature=0).

Persona consistency measures whether an agent’s utterance aligns with their assigned persona/background. The judge outputs YES (contradiction, score=0) or NO (consistent, score=1).

Template Variables:

  • •

    [SCENARIO_DESC] – Domain context (e.g., ”This is a tutoring conversation”)

  • •

    [SPEAKER_ROLE] – Agent role (e.g., ”Student”, ”Patient”, ”Agent 2”)

  • •

    [SPEAKER_BACKSTORY] – Full persona/background description assigned to agent

  • •

    [SPEAKER_LINE] – The specific utterance being evaluated

Appendix F Training Setup

We employ two 8B-parameter instruction-tuned base models: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [Grattafiori et al., 2024] and Qwen3-8B [Yang et al., 2025]. For computational efficiency, we limit the maximum context length to 4096 tokens during training. Models are fine-tuned for 3 epochs using the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of 5×10−65\times 10^{-6}, 0.01 weight decay, and a cosine schedule with 3% warmup, and trained using bfloat16 precision. Training is distributed across NVIDIA A100 GPUs using Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP). Llama-3.1 is trained with an effective batch size of 64, while Qwen3 utilizes an effective batch size of 128.

Appendix G Qualitative Analysis

This section provides an in-depth qualitative examination of persona consistency across different partial policy gradient methods. We present extensive dialogue examples that illustrate the key phenomena discussed in the main paper: 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base persona drift, 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG oscillation patterns, stability of K-step lookahead policies, and domain-specific optimal policies.

Example Selection. We curated representative dialogues from our test trajectories across three domains (Education, Therapy, Chatting), two model architectures (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B), and seven policies (𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base, 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG, 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG, 𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG, 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG, 𝟺−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 4\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG, 𝟻−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 5\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG). Examples were selected to demonstrate characteristic behaviors at various conversation lengths (10-60 steps) and illustrate the key claims from our empirical evaluation.

Visual Notation. We employ color-coded boxes to enhance readability:

  • •

    Cyan background: Response consistent with assigned persona

  • •

    Red background: Response contradicts persona or prior statements

  • •

    Orange background: Ambiguous or borderline consistency

  • •

    Blue annotations: Key observations and contradictions

  • •

    Yellow highlighting: Specific phrases that reveal inconsistency

Persona Display. Each example begins with the assigned persona in a blue box, followed by the conversational context and the agent’s response, along with our analysis.

G.1 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base Persona Drift: Monotonic Degradation

Motivation. In Tables 1, 2 and 3, we demonstrated quantitatively that unmodified 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base models achieve significantly lower persona consistency compared to RL-optimized policies. Here, we provide qualitative evidence for why this occurs and how the degradation manifests in actual conversations. Understanding the failure modes of 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base policies motivates our partial policy gradient framework and demonstrates the necessity of temporal credit assignment for persona consistency.

Observation. We present side-by-side comparisons of early conversation steps (steps 3-8) versus late steps (steps 38-51) for the same persona under 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base policy. The key phenomenon is monotonic degradation: personas that are initially maintained correctly systematically erode as conversation length increases. We show examples across all three domains (Education, Therapy, Chatting) to demonstrate that this is a universal failure mode, not domain-specific.

Interpretation. These examples illustrate the quantitative findings in Tables 1, 2, 3, where 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base achieves 0.425-0.478 PC across domains on Llama-3.1-8B, compared to 0.690-0.929 for optimal 𝙿𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPG methods. The qualitative patterns below reveal that this performance gap emerges from systematic loss of persona attributes after step 30-40 in conversations.

Education Domain: Learning Preference Abandonment

This example demonstrates how educational personas with specific learning preferences (visual vs. abstract) degrade under 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base. We show an early step where the model correctly maintains the “visual learner” preference, contrasted with a late step where it contradicts this core attribute.

Interpretation: At step 3, the model correctly expresses the visual learning preference (“Could you maybe draw out…?”, “A diagram… would help me see”). However, by step 42, the same persona explicitly contradicts this, stating “I’d rather just work through the abstract notation” and “I can follow the algebraic manipulations better than visual representations.” This is a direct reversal of the defining learning preference. This degradation contributes to the low 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base PC score of 0.425 in Education (Table 1).

Interpretation: At step 8, the model appropriately expresses test anxiety (“timed tests make me panic”) and requests untimed practice. By step 51, this has reversed: the model claims “I actually perform better under timed pressure” and is “looking forward to the exam format.” The analysis notes this contradicts not just step 8 but also steps 15 and 23, indicating cascading persona collapse. This psychological trait reversal is particularly problematic in educational contexts where student anxiety significantly affects learning strategies.

Therapy Domain: Mental Health Background Contradictions

Therapy personas involve complex psychological profiles with multiple interrelated facts (mental health history, coping mechanisms, social preferences). We demonstrate that 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base exhibits particularly severe drift in this domain, with fundamental personality traits reversing (introversion for extroversion). This explains why Therapy shows the lowest 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base performance (0.465 PC) across all three domains in our experiments.

Chatting Domain: Biographical Inconsistencies

Chatting personas consist of interconnected biographical details (profession, pets, diet, hobbies). Unlike education or therapy, these are concrete factual attributes rather than preferences or psychological states. However, 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base still fails to maintain consistency, demonstrating that persona drift is not limited to abstract traits but also affects simple factual information. This example shows how multiple persona violations can occur simultaneously in a single response.

G.2 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG Oscillation: Unstable Recovery Patterns

Motivation. Having established that 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base exhibits monotonic degradation, we now examine 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG (greedy policy gradient), which optimizes for immediate per-step persona consistency rewards. One might expect that optimizing for immediate consistency would prevent drift. However, our quantitative results in Figure 2 reveal that 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG exhibits characteristic oscillation patterns rather than smooth consistency. Here we provide qualitative evidence for why this occurs.

Observation. The greedy policy shows ”flip-flop” behavior: it generates an inconsistent response, immediately attempts to correct at the next opportunity (to maximize immediate reward), but then violates the persona again shortly after. We visualize this with a binary consistency plot showing alternating 0s and 1s, contrasted with the stable performance of 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG. The key insight is that without lookahead, the policy cannot anticipate that corrections now may lead to future inconsistencies.

Interpretation. This oscillation explains why 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG achieves moderate average PC (0.685 in Therapy, Table 2) through repeated recovery attempts, but exhibits high variance and instability visible in the residual plots (Figure 2). In contrast, 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG achieves 0.780 PC with smooth, stable consistency.

Ripple Patterns in Therapy Domain

We show a complete trajectory for a commitment-phobic patient persona, where 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG alternates between correct (PC=1) and contradictory (PC=0) responses across 13 measured steps. We contrast this with 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG, which maintains consistency throughout.

𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG Trajectory Showing Oscillation (Qwen3-8B):

G.3 K-Step Lookahead Stability

Motivation. We have shown that 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base degrades monotonically and 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG oscillates. Now we demonstrate that policies with bounded lookahead horizons (𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG and 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG) achieve stable, smooth consistency across extended conversations. This section provides qualitative evidence for the flat residual patterns observed in Figure 2 and the high PC scores in Tables 1, 2, 3.

Observation. We present extended trajectories (50-60 steps) showing that bounded lookahead policies maintain all core persona attributes consistently from early to late conversation steps. Unlike 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base (which degrades) and 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG (which oscillates), these policies demonstrate sustained coherence without flip-flopping. We show two domain-specific examples: 𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG in Chatting and 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG in Therapy, corresponding to the optimal policies identified in our quantitative analysis.

Key Mechanism. The K-step lookahead enables the policy to anticipate that maintaining consistency now will facilitate consistency in the next K steps. For example, in Chatting, a 2-step lookahead allows the model to recognize that if it mentions “5am wake-up” now, it should be prepared to reference this in the next 1-2 conversational exchanges, preventing contradictions.

𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG Success in Chatting Domain

We show a marathon runner + plant enthusiast persona maintained across 55 steps under 𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG. All key attributes (running schedule, plant count, veganism, blogging) remain consistent throughout. This demonstrates why 𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG achieves 0.929 PC in Chatting (Table 3).

Extended Trajectory with 𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG (Qwen3-8B) - Multiple Turns:

𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG Success in Therapy Domain

Therapy requires longer lookahead than Chatting because emotional states and therapeutic progress unfold over multiple conversational exchanges. We demonstrate that 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG maintains complex psychological states (postpartum depression symptoms: guilt, disconnection, stigma concerns) consistently across 52 steps, while allowing appropriate evolution (small improvements) that remain persona-consistent.

G.4 Domain-Specific Optimal Policies

Motivation. A central finding of our work is that different domains require different credit assignment horizons. Tables 1, 2, 3 show that Education favors full planning (𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG: 0.913 PC), Therapy favors 3-step lookahead (𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG: 0.780 PC), and Chatting favors 2-step lookahead (𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG: 0.929 PC). But why do these domain-specific optima exist? This section provides qualitative evidence.

Observation. We show: (1) 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG succeeds in Education by maintaining long-range psychological coherence (anxiety + growth mindset across 32 steps), while 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG loses these distant connections. (2) 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG fails in Therapy by over-planning, creating unrealistic recovery arcs (“transcended desire” or total collapse), while 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG maintains realistic day-by-day progress. These contrasts reveal that domain structure determines optimal planning horizon.

Key Insight. Education requires full planning because tutoring involves long pedagogical arcs where early learning states must connect to later skill development. Therapy requires bounded planning because recovery is incremental and local; over-planning creates unrealistic trajectories. Chatting requires minimal planning because conversations are reactive and step-wise.

Full Planning Success in Education

We demonstrate how 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG maintains multiple interconnected persona threads (math anxiety from high school trauma, growth mindset, teaching style preferences) across distant conversational steps (step 18 → step 32), enabling complex callbacks and psychological coherence that 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG cannot achieve.

Comparison: 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG Loses Long-Range Coherence:

Full Planning Instability in Therapy

Conversely, we show that the same full planning approach (𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG) that excels in Education fails in Therapy. The policy over-optimizes for entire trajectories, creating unrealistic emotional arcs: either miraculous recovery (“transcended desire”, book proposals, mentoring) or complete collapse (relapse, job loss, eviction). In contrast, 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG maintains realistic, gradual progress. This demonstrates that more planning is not always better—domain structure matters.

𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG Maintains Realistic Consistency:

G.5 Cross-Model Consistency and Temporal Progression

Motivation. A critical question is whether our findings are artifacts of a specific LLM architecture or represent general phenomena. We address this by comparing identical persona-policy combinations across two architectures: Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B. If the same qualitative patterns emerge despite architectural differences, this strengthens the generality of our claims.

Observation. We show the same persona (freelance designer new to Austin) under the same policy (𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG) on both models at the same conversation step (step 31). Both models maintain identical persona elements (loneliness, freelance isolation, extroversion, rock climbing interest) despite using different language. This demonstrates that 𝙿𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPG stability is architecture-independent.

Interpretation. Tables 1, 2, 3 show that policy rankings are consistent across Llama and Qwen: 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG wins in Education for both, 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG wins in Therapy for both, 𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG wins in Chatting for both. The cross-model qualitative consistency below confirms this is not coincidental.

To validate that our findings generalize across LLM architectures, we compare identical persona-policy combinations on both Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B. While absolute performance differs (as seen in Tables 1, 2, 3), the qualitative patterns remain remarkably consistent.

Temporal Progression Analysis

Beyond cross-model validation, we examine temporal dynamics: how does the same persona evolve from early (step 12) to mid (step 32) to late (step 54) conversation stages under different policies? This visualizes the monotonic degradation of 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base versus the sustained stability of 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG across 54 steps, providing a clear visual narrative of the temporal credit assignment problem.

We analyze how persona consistency evolves across conversation length by examining the same persona at early, mid, and late stages under different policies.

G.6 Statistical Efficiency Manifestation

Motivation. Figure 3 demonstrates quantitatively that simpler policies (𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG) achieve better statistical efficiency in low-data regimes than complex policies (𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG), while the gap closes with sufficient data. This reflects the variance-bias tradeoff in gradient estimation (Theorem 5). Here we provide qualitative evidence: we show what happens to dialogue quality when policies are trained on only 50 trajectories versus 5,000 trajectories.

Observation. With only 50 training trajectories, 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG generates coherent, persona-consistent responses while 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG produces completely nonsensical outputs (vegan chef → carnivore steakhouse), demonstrating catastrophic failure. With 5,000 trajectories, both policies succeed. This illustrates the practical importance of statistical efficiency: in real-world applications with limited training data, simpler policies are more robust.

Connection to Theory. This qualitative phenomenon directly demonstrates Theorem 5: 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG has a simpler gradient estimator with lower variance, enabling faster concentration from limited samples. 𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG has higher variance requiring more data to converge, leading to complete failure in low-data regimes.

Our main paper (Figure 3) demonstrates that simpler policies learn more efficiently in low-data regimes. Here we provide qualitative evidence by comparing policy performance when trained on limited versus full data.

Low-Data Regime (50 Trajectories): 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG Wins

High-Data Regime (5,000 Trajectories): Both Succeed

Broader Implications. These 78 detailed examples provide rich qualitative support for our quantitative findings in Tables 1, 2, 3 and Figures 2, 3. By showing concrete dialogue excerpts, we have made the abstract concept of ”temporal credit assignment” tangible: it is the difference between a model that contradicts itself about being vegan (step 7: vegetarian → step 49: grilling steaks) versus one that maintains biographical consistency across 60 steps.

The examples illustrate why different credit assignment horizons succeed or fail in different domains, offering insights beyond aggregate numerical metrics. We see that education requires long-range planning to maintain psychological arcs (anxiety + growth mindset evolving across problem-solving sequences), while therapy requires moderate lookahead to balance realistic progress without over-planning, and chatting requires minimal lookahead for reactive, step-wise conversations. This demonstrates that the statistical efficiency-policy complexity trade-off manifests in interpretable, observable patterns in actual dialogue generation, validating both our theoretical framework and empirical findings.

G.7 Quantitative Overlays on Qualitative Examples

We further analyze systematic failure taxonomies, and cross-domain validation. Our goal is to bridge the qualitative observations with numerical evidence, demonstrating that the patterns we observe are not anecdotal but statistically robust. Throughout this section, we use windowed persona consistency (PC) metrics: since PC is binary (0 or 1) at each step, we report aggregate PC scores over sliding windows (e.g., PC over steps 1-10, 11-20, etc.) to quantify drift patterns. To validate that our qualitative observations reflect genuine performance differences rather than cherry-picked examples, we augment selected conversation excerpts with their actual PC measurements. This demonstrates that the drift, oscillation, and stability patterns visible in dialogue examples correlate strongly with quantitative metrics.

Education: Quantified Preference Abandonment

We revisit the “visual learner” persona and overlay it with step-wise consistency measurements. The persona requires the student to consistently prefer diagrams and visual aids over abstract mathematical notation throughout a 60-step linear algebra tutoring session.

Why This Matters: These numbers confirm that the linear degradation pattern in 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base suggests systematic failure to maintain persona constraints over extended interactions, while 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG’s stability demonstrates that temporal credit assignment directly addresses this failure mode.

Therapy: Oscillation Quantified

In Appendix G, we qualitatively observed that 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG exhibits “flip-flop” behavior in therapy scenarios, where personas alternate between consistent and contradictory states across steps. Here we quantify this oscillation by measuring step-wise PC scores (binary: 1 = consistent, 0 = inconsistent) and counting “flips” - transitions from PC=1 to PC=0 or vice versa. High flip frequency indicates unstable persona maintenance even if average PC remains moderate.

Statistical Validation Across Trajectories: We computed flip frequencies across 18 therapy trajectories with emotionally complex personas (commitment issues, trauma, relationship anxiety). 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG exhibits mean flip frequency of 0.18±0.090.18\pm 0.09 per step, while 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG achieves 0.05±0.030.05\pm 0.03 (p<0.001p<0.001, Mann-Whitney U test). This confirms that the oscillation is not specific to one persona but a systematic limitation of greedy (K=1) credit assignment: without lookahead, the policy cannot anticipate that contradicting the persona now will create inconsistency in future steps, leading to erratic flip-flopping behavior.

Average PC scores alone (as reported in Table 1) can mask instability. A policy with PC=0.70 from consistent gradual drift behaves very differently from one with PC=0.70 from chaotic oscillations. This flip frequency metric reveals that 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG’s moderate performance in therapy (0.67 PC, Table 2) is qualitatively worse than it appears numerically, because the inconsistencies are unpredictable and jarring rather than gradual.

G.8 Common Failure Modes and Error Taxonomy

Beyond measuring when and how much persona drift occurs, we investigate what fails. By manually analyzing 247 conversation trajectories where 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base achieved PC << 0.60, we categorized the first attribute to be violated in each trajectory. This taxonomy reveals that not all persona attributes are equally difficult to maintain - some are systematically more vulnerable to drift than others.

Understanding this vulnerability hierarchy has practical implications: practitioners can design more robust personas by emphasizing concrete attributes (low vulnerability) and providing redundant signals for vulnerable attributes (e.g., mentioning profession multiple times in persona description).

G.9 Failure Mode Taxonomy

We categorize persona attributes into five types and measure what percentage of failures originate from each category. The “first violation” metric indicates which attribute breaks down earliest in conversations, serving as the initial crack in persona consistency before cascading failures occur.

Implication for 𝙿𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPG Methods: This taxonomy explains why lookahead helps. Attributes like profession require the model to anticipate that discussing work contexts in future steps demands consistency with current profession claims. Short-sighted policies (𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base, 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG) don’t plan ahead for these multi-step dependencies, while 𝙺−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt K\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG methods explicitly optimize for consistency across K future steps, directly addressing the vulnerability of profession/family attributes.

G.10 Error Propagation Cascade

A critical question is whether persona violations occur as isolated incidents or trigger cascading failures. We analyze a case study where a single initial error at step 23 compounds through subsequent steps, demonstrating how 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base policies can spiral into complete persona collapse while 𝙺−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt K\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG methods contain errors through early self-correction.

The key insight here is that errors create false context for future responses. Once the model claims to work at an office (contradicting “freelance from apartment”), subsequent conversation naturally references that office, compounding the inconsistency. Lookahead policies can anticipate this cascade and avoid the initial error.

This case study demonstrates that the credit assignment problem in persona consistency is not just about individual step quality, but about preventing error cascades. The 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base policy achieves PC=1 for 22 consecutive steps before a single mistake triggers collapse. This validates our theoretical motivation in Section 1: without lookahead, policies cannot anticipate how current errors propagate through future context, leading to systemic failure.

G.11 Cross-Domain Persona Transfer

A potential confound in our main results (Tables 1, 2 and 3) is that different domains might have different personas in addition to different conversational structures. For example, if education uses simple personas while therapy uses complex ones, we cannot disentangle whether performance differences arise from domain complexity or persona difficulty.

To address this, we conduct controlled cross-domain experiments: we take the same persona attributes (e.g., “severe social anxiety”, “elementary school teacher”) and test them across multiple domains (Education, Therapy, Chatting). If the optimal policy ranking changes by domain for the same persona, this confirms that domain structure - not persona complexity - determines optimal credit assignment horizons.

This analysis validates that the domain-specific recommendations in Tables 1, 2 and 3 are driven by conversational structure (planning depth, step dependencies) rather than artifacts of persona selection.

Professional Identity Transfer

As a second cross-domain validation, we test the same professional identity (“elementary school teacher”) across Education and Chatting domains. Recall from our failure taxonomy (above) that profession is the most vulnerable attribute (34% of first violations). Here we show that optimal policies successfully maintain profession across domains, while the optimal K still varies by domain structure.

Cross-Domain Insight: Both optimal policies successfully maintain professional identity (PC >> 0.90), confirming that 𝙿𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PPG methods address the vulnerability of profession attributes identified in our taxonomy. However, the optimal lookahead horizon differs by domain: Education requires long-range planning (𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG) because professional background must be integrated into multi-step learning strategies (e.g., “As an engineer, I know this concept from studying this in undergraduate Chemistry…” affects how future content should be explained). Chatting requires only short-range consistency (𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG) because profession mentions are more isolated (e.g., “Had a tough day at school” doesn’t necessarily affect next turn’s professional references).

Validation: This confirms that optimal K is determined by conversational structure (how far ahead profession must be considered), not by whether profession is inherently hard to maintain.

G.12 Error Recovery Dynamics

Beyond preventing errors initially, we investigate whether policies can recover from inconsistencies when they do occur. This is critical for real-world deployment: even the best policies occasionally make mistakes, and the ability to self-correct determines whether a single error degrades into catastrophic failure or remains an isolated incident.

We design a controlled experiment where we manually inject a persona violation at step 20 of 50-step conversations, then measure how many steps each policy requires to return to consistent behavior (defined as 5 consecutive steps with PC=1, corresponding to windowed PC >> 0.80 over steps 21-25).

Key Takeaway: This analysis reveals a fundamental tradeoff in credit assignment: longer horizons improve consistency and reduce error frequency, but can slow recovery when errors do occur. 𝟸−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG and 𝟹−𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙−𝙿𝙶\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG strike the best balance for most scenarios. Importantly, any lookahead is dramatically better than 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎\color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base (which never recovers), validating that temporal credit assignment is essential for robust persona consistency.
